text: With the stack chosen, this is the first real design decision: the shape of the warehouse itself. One fact table, fact_sales, surrounded by three dimensions — dim_date, dim_store, dim_product. Get the grain right here, on a whiteboard, and everything downstream just works. Get it wrong, and it's a rebuild, not an edit.

Everything starts from one sentence: one row in fact_sales equals one store's sales of one product on one day. Every measure, every dimension attribute, has to resolve to exactly one value at that grain — if it doesn't, the design is wrong before a single CREATE TABLE statement runs.
dim_date is pre-populated years in advance — fiscal week, day name, weekend flag, all computed once. dim_store is small and slow-changing, just fourteen rows, nothing fancy.

dim_product is where the real decision lives. Price and category change over time, and the VP will eventually ask about margin on a promotion from last year. Overwriting the product row in place destroys that history — so dim_product is Type 2: a new row, a new surrogate key, every time price or category changes.

That's exactly why we use surrogate keys instead of natural keys. The SKU code stays constant forever; the surrogate key changes with each new version of the row. A historical sale keeps pointing at the product attributes that were true the day it happened.

fact_sales holds almost nothing but foreign keys and measures — date_key, store_key, product_key, quantity, gross amount, net amount. That key triple is the fact table's natural identity, and it has to match the grain sentence exactly.

Draw it as an actual star before moving on — one fact table in the center, three lines out to the dimensions. If you ever want to draw a line between two dimensions directly, that's the sign something doesn't belong in a pure star. Next: planning how data actually gets into this shape, every single night.
